claim: Agent Skill Evolution (R-106; arXiv id from an AI review)
head: Agent Skill Evolution: How Revisions Affect Coding Agents JIAJIE WANG, The University of Arizona, USA YUTONG ZHAO, California State University, Long Beach, USA TIANLIN LI, Nanyang Technological University, Singapore HUASHAN CHEN, Institute of Information Engineering, Chinese Academy of Science, China JINFU CHEN, Wuhan University, China KEBIN PENG, East Carolina University, USA SEN HE, The University of Arizona, USA Agent Skills, the SKILL.md files that tell an LLM coding agent how a project works, are revised like code, yet what a revision does to the agent is unknown. From 2,608 first/last revision pairs of 3,159 Skills, we characterize how Skills evolve and how they change together with the configuration of the agent’s harness. We then focus on rule changes, revisions that add or remove a rule we can check automatically, such as “run allium check”. We measure their effect on 21 models in single answers and on four agents in a sandbox, and their cost on 20 of these models and the four agents. Most revisions (55%) change a rule or procedure, and commits that revise a Skill change harness files such as CLAUDE.md more often than other commits of the same size. Across 16 open-weight models, an added rule raises compliance in a single answer by +0.41 on average. Across the four agents, the rate at which the agent takes the required action rises by +0.23 on average (+0.16 to +0.36), and for the three agents that blind judges assessed, final correctness rises by +0.10 on average (+

An annotator labelled 100 of these pairs by hand, drawn stratified by the judgement of Qwen 3-32B (greedy decoding) on whether completing the commit needs the rule, and reweighted them to all 1,454 pairs. Of these commits, 25% need the rule (95% CI 14–40%; 18–46% by how unclear pairs are counted; Table S36). Automated proxies under-count (Table S35). As a scenario, suppose that the conditional effects hold unchanged on in-scope requests that need the rule and are zero on those that do not. An in-scope request would then gain about 0.10 in single-answer compliance (0.25 × 0.41; 95% CI of the product 0.05–0.17) and about 0.06 in the required action of the four sandbox agents (0.25 × 0.23), while every request reads the revision’s tokens. Three practices follow for maintainers. Add a rule when it gives the agent information the Skill lacks. Before deleting a rule, check that the agent should no longer follow it, since deletions are followed too. Size a Skill for the smallest model that will read it, since the model’s release year matters less. 7.3 Relation to Prior Findings Jiang et al. We also let the agent decide whether to read the Skill (§5.2.4), and pose single-step probes inside long contexts that resemble an agent’s (§5.1.7). 3.4 Evaluation Metrics Effectiveness has three levels. Directive compliance in one answer is Level 1 (string check), the required action of an executing agent is Level 2, and final correctness of the produced artifact is Level 3. Level 1 covers every model but also credits an answer that repeats a token it was shown, so it includes information exposure as well as directive following. ed. 5 RQ2: How Does Skill Evolution Affect Task Effectiveness? Motivation and Approach. A maintainer revises a Skill to change an agent’s behaviour, which can affect task effectiveness. We study rule changes, a narrower class within the 55.0% of revisions that RQ1’s classifier marks as changing a rule or procedure; that classifier misses most MUST/NEVER and conditional lines (recall 0.18 and 0.19). Of the 2,608 revisions, 1,074 (41%) add at least one directive that names a command, path or identifier. We focus on such rules because revisions that change only prose or only examples barely move compliance with a Skill’s existing rules. On the 154 dilution probes whose revision changes only prose or examples, four models (Qwen 2.5-7B, Qwen 3-8B, Qwen 3.5-9B and Phi-4-mini) change compliance by +0.017 [+0.002, +0.034], within an equivalence margin of 0.08 fixed before the run (per-model data-derived bounds at most 0.06), while the Skill body itself adds +0.57 over none (Table S12). We measure effectiveness at the three levels of §3.4 and supplement the string check with a token-only control, action traces and blind judgements. For closed models we report token cost for the four Claude models, whose reported usage we could match to our prompts. 6.1 Single-Step Setting 6.1.1 A revision adds input tokens but shortens the answer. Input grows because the new version is longer (Table 6), and output shrinks, because a model told which command to run answers more concisely than one that hedges. In juxt/allium, a rule to run allium check shrinks the answer from 201 to 81 tokens and raises compliance from 0.07 to 0.99. The marginal cost of a revision is therefore almost entirely input. Counting input and output, a request uses 17% more tokens on the open models and 24 to 27% more on the four Claude models (Table 7). At list prices, where output , Vol. 1, No. 1, Article . For each added rule and each model, a rule–model pair, we checked whether compliance changed and whether tokens increased. With five samples per condition, compliance moves in steps of 0.2. Compliance improves in 58% of pairs. In 20%, the prompt grows but we detect no change in compliance, and we call these overhead candidates (repository-clustered 95% CI 16.1–24.2%; 18–27% under six alternative thresholds).
